comment: Chemistry multiple choice for the Year 11 modules 11-17. answer is the 0-based index.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Why do lithium, sodium and potassium have similar chemical reactions?
options: They all have one electron in their outer shell
They all have the same number of shells
They all have the same number of protons
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Reactions happen at the outer shell. All Group 1 atoms have one outer electron, so they react in the same way.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: What are the products when sodium reacts with water?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂. A Group 1 metal and water always give a metal hydroxide and hydrogen.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Phenolphthalein is added to the solution left after sodium reacts with water. What colour does it turn?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Phenolphthalein turns pink in alkali, and the solution contains OH⁻ ions. The 2024 mark scheme rejected red and purple.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Which observation is seen when potassium reacts with water but NOT when lithium does?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Potassium releases so much heat that the hydrogen ignites with a lilac flame. Lithium reacts too slowly for that.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: What is the final colour of universal indicator after sodium has reacted with the water it is in?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: The sodium hydroxide solution is alkaline, so universal indicator turns blue or purple.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Why does sodium melt into a ball when it reacts with water?
options: It reacts with oxygen dissolved in the water
The reaction is exothermic and sodium has a low melting point
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: The heat given out is enough to melt sodium, which melts at 98 °C.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Which is the correct order of reactivity, most reactive first?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Reactivity increases down Group 1, so potassium is the most reactive of the three.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Why is potassium more reactive than sodium?
options: Potassium has more protons, so it attracts electrons more strongly
Potassium has more outer electrons to lose
Potassium's outer electron is further from the nucleus, so it is less strongly attracted
Potassium has a smaller atomic radius
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Potassium has more shells, so its outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded. It is lost more easily.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Why are Group 1 metals stored under oil?
options: To stop them reacting with air and water
To make them easier to cut
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: The oil keeps oxygen and water away from the metal, so it does not tarnish or react.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: A freshly cut piece of lithium is shiny but slowly goes dull. What causes this?
options: It reacts with oxygen to form an oxide
It reacts with nitrogen to form a nitride
It melts in the warm air
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: The shiny metal reacts with oxygen in the air to form a dull oxide layer. This is called tarnishing.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: The melting points of Li, Na and K are 181 °C, 98 °C and 63 °C. Which is the best prediction for rubidium's melting point?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Melting point decreases down Group 1, so rubidium's must be below 63 °C. Its actual melting point is 39 °C.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: What is the formula of rubidium hydroxide?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Rubidium is in Group 1, so it forms Rb⁺ ions. One Rb⁺ balances one OH⁻.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Which equation for lithium reacting with water is correctly balanced?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: There are two H atoms in H₂, so two LiOH and two H₂O are needed, and therefore two Li.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: 0.46 g of sodium reacts with water. How many moles of hydrogen are made? [Aᵣ of Na = 23]
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: 0.46 ÷ 23 = 0.020 mol of Na. Two Na give one H₂, so 0.010 mol of H₂ is made.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: What colour and state is chlorine at room temperature?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Chlorine is a pale yellow-green gas. Bromine is the red-brown liquid and iodine is the grey-black solid.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: What colour and state is bromine at room temperature?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Bromine is a red-brown liquid that gives off an orange-brown vapour.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: What colour is iodine vapour?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Solid iodine is grey-black, but when it is warmed it gives a purple vapour.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Which halogen has the palest colour?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Colour darkens down Group 7, so fluorine, at the top, is the palest (pale yellow).

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Which halogen is a solid at room temperature?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Melting points rise down Group 7. Iodine and astatine are solids, bromine is a liquid, and chlorine and fluorine are gases.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Why do the boiling points of the halogens increase down the group?
options: The intermolecular forces get stronger as the molecules get bigger
The atoms lose electrons more easily
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Boiling overcomes the forces between molecules. These get stronger as the molecules get larger. No covalent bonds are broken.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Chlorine water is added to potassium bromide solution. What is seen?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Chlorine is more reactive, so it displaces bromine, and bromine in solution is orange.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Bromine water is added to potassium chloride solution. What happens?
options: There is no change — it stays orange
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Bromine is less reactive than chlorine, so it cannot displace chlorine. The mixture stays orange.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Bromine water is added to potassium iodide solution. What colour does the solution become?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Bromine displaces iodine, and iodine in solution is brown.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Which mixture will NOT react?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Iodine is less reactive than bromine, so it cannot displace bromine from potassium bromide.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Which is the correct ionic equation for chlorine reacting with bromide ions?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Two Br⁻ ions make one Br₂ molecule, and Cl₂ becomes two Cl⁻ ions. Atoms and charges both balance.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: In the reaction Cl₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + I₂, which species is oxidised?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Iodide ions lose electrons to form iodine (2I⁻ → I₂ + 2e⁻). Loss of electrons is oxidation.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: In a halogen displacement reaction, what is the role of the more reactive halogen?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: The halogen takes electrons from the halide ion. It is reduced and acts as the oxidising agent.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: In the reaction between chlorine and potassium bromide solution, which ions are spectator ions?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: K⁺ ions are unchanged in the reaction, so they are left out of the ionic equation.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Which is the correct half-equation for chlorine in a displacement reaction?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Each chlorine atom gains one electron, so Cl₂ gains two electrons to form 2Cl⁻. This is reduction.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Why is fluorine more reactive than chlorine?
options: Fluorine's outer shell is closer to the nucleus, so it attracts an extra electron more strongly
Fluorine has more electrons in its outer shell
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Fluorine (2.7) has fewer shells than chlorine (2.8.7), so the nucleus pulls an incoming electron more strongly.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Going down Group 7, what happens to the reactivity of the halogens?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: The outer shell gets further from the nucleus, so an extra electron is gained less readily.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: What is the best prediction for what happens when chlorine water is added to sodium astatide solution?
options: No reaction, because astatine is more reactive
Astatine is displaced, because chlorine is more reactive
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Astatine is at the bottom of Group 7, so it is the least reactive halogen. Chlorine displaces it.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: What is the correct equation for lithium reacting with chlorine?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Chlorine is diatomic (Cl₂) and lithium chloride is LiCl, so two lithium atoms are needed.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Why is neon unreactive?
options: It has a full outer shell, so it does not need to lose, gain or share electrons
It is a gas at room temperature
It has one electron in its outer shell
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Neon is 2.8, with a full outer shell. That is stable, so it does not form bonds.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Helium has only 2 outer electrons. Why is it still unreactive?
options: 2 electrons fill its only shell, so its outer shell is full
It is too light to react
Its electrons are too far from the nucleus
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Helium's first shell holds a maximum of 2 electrons, so helium has a full outer shell like the other noble gases.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Magnesium is used to extract titanium from TiCl₄ in a container of argon. Why argon rather than air?
options: Argon is unreactive, whereas oxygen in air would oxidise the magnesium
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Argon does not react with the hot metal. In air, oxygen would react with the magnesium and titanium.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Which is the least reactive gas in the atmosphere?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Argon is a noble gas with a full outer shell, so it is the least reactive gas in air.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Noble gases exist as single atoms. What is the word for this?
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Noble gas atoms do not bond to each other, so they exist as separate atoms. They are monatomic.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Why are filament light bulbs filled with argon?
options: The hot filament does not react with argon
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: Argon is unreactive. In air, the hot filament would react with oxygen and burn out.

11-groups-1-7-and-0.q: Which statement about Group 1 and Group 7 is correct?
options: Both groups get more reactive down the group
Group 1 atoms gain electrons; Group 7 atoms lose electrons
Both groups get less reactive down the group
Group 1 gets more reactive down the group; Group 7 gets less reactive
11-groups-1-7-and-0.explain: The outer shell gets further from the nucleus in both groups. That makes losing an electron easier (Group 1) but gaining one harder (Group 7).

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: What is the approximate percentage by volume of nitrogen in dry air?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Dry air is about 78% nitrogen, which is roughly four-fifths. In 2024 the multiple-choice answer was given as 80%.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: What is the approximate percentage by volume of oxygen in dry air?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Oxygen is about 21%, roughly one-fifth of dry air. 0.9% is argon and 78% is nitrogen.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Which gas makes up about 1% of dry air?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Argon is about 0.9%, the trace gas with the highest percentage. Carbon dioxide is only about 0.04%.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Which of these gases has the lowest percentage by volume in dry air?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Carbon dioxide is about 0.04%, much less than argon (0.9%), oxygen (21%) or nitrogen (78%).

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Which gas is NOT normally found in the atmosphere?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Hydrogen is not normally found in the atmosphere (2022 Edexcel 2C Q1). The other three are all present.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Why is the composition of air usually given for DRY air?
options: Water vapour is a greenhouse gas
The amount of water vapour varies from place to place and day to day
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Water vapour changes a lot, so it is left out. That way the percentages of the other gases stay fixed.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Why does argon not react with hot copper or iron?
options: It has a full outer shell of electrons
It is a gas at room temperature
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Argon has a full outer shell, so it does not gain, lose or share electrons. Being a gas has nothing to do with it.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: In the iron wool and test tube experiment, why does water rise up the tube?
options: The iron dissolves in the water
The water evaporates into the tube
The iron uses up the oxygen, so the gas volume decreases
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Iron reacts with oxygen to form solid rust. The gas volume falls and water moves up to fill the space.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Why must the iron wool be wet in the rusting experiment?
options: Water is needed for iron to rust
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Iron needs both oxygen and water to rust, so the iron must be wet for the oxygen to be used up.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Why is iron powder better than an iron nail for finding the % of oxygen in air?
options: Powder has a larger surface area, so it reacts faster
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: A larger surface area means more collisions per second, so the oxygen is used up sooner. The final result is the same.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: What colour is rust?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Rust is brown (orange-brown or red-brown was also allowed). The 2022 scheme ignored 'red' on its own.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: What is the formula of the iron oxide in rust?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide. Fe³⁺ and O²⁻ give Fe₂O₃.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: A gas column in an inverted tube falls from 75 mm to 30 mm as the oxygen is used. What is the percentage of oxygen?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: The decrease is 45 mm, and 45 ÷ 75 × 100 = 60%. 40% is the gas left, which scored only 1 of 2 in 2023.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: A flask and tube hold 260 cm³. The syringe falls from 90 cm³ to 22 cm³. What is the % oxygen?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Oxygen = 68 cm³ and total air = 260 + 90 = 350 cm³, so 68 ÷ 350 × 100 = 19.4%. 26.2% leaves out the syringe air.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: In the gas-syringe method, what is the total starting volume of air?
options: The flask volume plus the starting syringe reading
The flask volume minus the final syringe reading
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: The flask and syringe are connected, so the iron removes oxygen from both. The total is the apparatus plus the starting syringe reading.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: How do you know all the oxygen has reacted in the heated-copper method?
options: The syringe readings stay the same
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: When repeated passes give the same reading, no more oxygen is being removed.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Why is the copper heated in the two-syringe experiment?
options: To increase the rate so the copper reacts with the oxygen
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Cold copper reacts with oxygen far too slowly. Heating gives the particles enough energy to react quickly.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: What is the black solid formed when copper reacts with oxygen?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: 2Cu + O₂ → 2CuO, which is black copper(II) oxide. The mark scheme rejected copper(I) oxide.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Why should the apparatus cool to room temperature before the final syringe reading?
options: Warm gas takes up a larger volume
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Gas expands when hot. A warm final reading is too big, which makes the % oxygen too low.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Syringe A reads 78 cm³ at the start and 58 cm³ at the end. The tube holds 175 cm³. What is the % oxygen in the mixture?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Oxygen = 20 cm³ and total = 175 + 78 = 253 cm³, so 20 ÷ 253 × 100 = 7.9% (2022 Jan Edexcel 1C Q4).

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Which non-metal is named in the spec for finding the % of oxygen in air?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: The spec names iron (a metal) and phosphorus (a non-metal) for this experiment.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Which observation is seen when magnesium burns in oxygen?
options: A blue flame and a choking gas
A bright white light and a white powder
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Magnesium burns with a bright white light and leaves white magnesium oxide powder. 'White precipitate' was rejected.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Which is the correct balanced equation for magnesium burning?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Oxygen is O₂ and magnesium oxide is MgO, so you need 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: What are the state symbols in 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Magnesium is a solid, oxygen a gas and magnesium oxide a solid: (s), (g), (s), as in the school's 2025 Q4(b).

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: What is seen when sulfur burns in oxygen?
options: A blue flame and a colourless, choking gas
An orange flame and black smoke
No flame, just a brown solid
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Sulfur burns with a blue flame to form sulfur dioxide, a colourless gas with a choking smell.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: What is the product when hydrogen burns in oxygen?
options: Hydrogen oxide gas that is acidic
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. The only product is water.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: What type of oxide does a metal form?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Metal oxides are basic. Those that dissolve give alkaline solutions with a pH above 7.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Sulfur dioxide dissolves in water. What would the solution do to blue litmus?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: SO₂ is an acidic oxide, so its solution contains H⁺ ions and turns blue litmus red.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Which ion makes a solution of sulfur dioxide acidic?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Acidic solutions contain hydrogen ions, H⁺ (school 2021 Q10(c)).

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: An element conducts electricity and its oxide gives a solution of pH 11. The element is most likely:
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Conducting electricity and forming a basic oxide are both properties of metals.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Which element forms a basic oxide?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Lithium is a metal, so its oxide is basic. This was the 2024 Edexcel 1C Q1(a) answer. The others are non-metals.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Where are non-metals found in the Periodic Table?
options: On the right, beyond the stepped line
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Non-metals are on the right of the stepped line (plus hydrogen). Metals are on the left and in the centre.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Which non-metal element conducts electricity?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Graphite has delocalised electrons, so it conducts. It is the usual exception to 'non-metals do not conduct'.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: What type of reaction happens when copper(II) carbonate is heated?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Heat breaks one substance into two: CuCO₃ → CuO + CO₂. This is thermal decomposition.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: What colour change is seen when copper(II) carbonate is heated?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Copper(II) carbonate is green, and copper(II) oxide is black. Both 2022 and 2023 asked this.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Which equation shows the thermal decomposition of copper(II) carbonate?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: A metal carbonate decomposes to the metal oxide and carbon dioxide: CuCO₃ → CuO + CO₂.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: 7.40 g of XCO₃ gives off 2.20 g of CO₂ when heated. What is the Mᵣ of XCO₃?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: n(CO₂) = 2.20 ÷ 44 = 0.05 mol = n(XCO₃), so Mᵣ = 7.40 ÷ 0.05 = 148. Then Aᵣ(X) = 88, which is strontium.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Which of these reactions produces carbon dioxide?
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon gives carbon dioxide and water. Mg + HCl gives hydrogen.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Why is an increasing amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere a problem?
options: It is a greenhouse gas that may contribute to climate change
It is the main cause of acid rain
It reduces the amount of nitrogen
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: CO₂ traps heat in the atmosphere. Mark schemes reject answers about the ozone layer and ignore acid rain.

12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.q: Which is an accepted effect of increasing carbon dioxide levels?
options: More ozone in the upper atmosphere
Rising sea levels from melting ice caps
12-gases-in-the-atmosphere.explain: Climate change leads to melting ice caps, rising sea levels, flooding and wildfires. Oceans becoming more acidic is also accepted.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Which two substances must both be present for iron to rust?
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Iron rusts only when both oxygen (air) and water are present. Salt speeds rusting up but is not needed.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: What is the chemical name for rust?
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide, simplified formula Fe₂O₃. Iron(II) oxide is rejected by the mark schemes.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: What type of reaction is the rusting of iron?
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Iron gains oxygen (and loses electrons) when it rusts, so rusting is oxidation.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Which metal is used to galvanise iron?
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Galvanising means coating iron or steel with a layer of zinc.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: A galvanised bucket is scratched through to the steel, but the steel does not rust. Why?
options: Zinc is more reactive than iron, so the zinc is oxidised instead of the iron
Zinc is less reactive than iron, so it seals the scratch
The zinc rusts instead of the iron
The scratch fills with zinc oxide paint
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Zinc is more reactive, so it corrodes (is oxidised) instead of the iron. Saying zinc 'rusts' is rejected — only iron rusts.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Which of these is a barrier method of rust prevention?
options: Connecting to a less reactive metal
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Greasing coats the iron so water and oxygen cannot reach it. Magnesium blocks are sacrificial protection, not a barrier.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Why are blocks of magnesium attached to the steel hull of a ship?
options: Magnesium is less reactive than iron, so it protects it
Magnesium is more reactive than iron, so it corrodes instead of the iron
Magnesium reacts with salt to make a waterproof layer
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: This is sacrificial protection: the more reactive magnesium is oxidised instead of the iron.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: In the rusting experiment, why is a layer of oil put on top of the boiled water?
options: To stop air dissolving back into the water
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Boiling removes dissolved air; the oil layer stops oxygen dissolving back in, so the tube has water but no oxygen.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: What is the job of anhydrous calcium chloride in a rusting experiment?
options: It absorbs water vapour, keeping the air dry
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Anhydrous calcium chloride is a drying agent; that tube shows iron does not rust without water.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Which tube will show rust after a week?
options: Nail in boiled water under a layer of oil
Nail in tap water, open to the air
Nail in dry air with calcium chloride, stoppered
Nail in a sealed tube of dry nitrogen
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Only the tube with both water and oxygen rusts.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Why does iron powder rust faster than an iron nail?
options: Powder is more reactive than iron in a nail
Powder has a larger surface area
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: A larger surface area gives a faster reaction — the same metal, just more of it exposed.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: What is observed when magnesium ribbon is added to dilute hydrochloric acid?
options: Vigorous fizzing and the tube gets warm
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Magnesium is high in the series, so it reacts fast with acid to give hydrogen; the reaction is exothermic.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Which metal does NOT react with dilute sulfuric acid?
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series, so it cannot displace hydrogen from acids.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: What are the products when zinc reacts with dilute sulfuric acid?
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Metal + acid → salt + hydrogen: Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Which is the correct equation for iron reacting with dilute sulfuric acid?
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Iron forms iron(II) sulfate and hydrogen with dilute sulfuric acid; the equation is balanced 1:1:1:1.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Give the word equation for aluminium reacting with hydrochloric acid.
options: aluminium + hydrochloric acid → aluminium chlorine + hydrogen
aluminium + hydrochloric acid → aluminium oxide + hydrogen
aluminium + hydrochloric acid → aluminium chloride + water
aluminium + hydrochloric acid → aluminium chloride + hydrogen
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Hydrochloric acid makes chlorides, and a metal with acid gives hydrogen.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Why is the reaction of sodium with dilute hydrochloric acid not done in school?
options: Sodium does not react with acid
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Sodium is very high in the series; its reaction with acid is violent. 'Vigorous' or 'volatile' alone scored nothing in 2024.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Metal A reacts very fast with water. Metal B does not react with water but fizzes slowly in acid. Metal C does not react with either. Which could B be?
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: B is above hydrogen but does not react with cold water — zinc or iron fits. Potassium and sodium react fast with water; gold does not react with acid.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: What forms when magnesium reacts with steam?
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: With steam the product is the oxide: Mg + H₂O → MgO + H₂.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Which is the balanced equation for calcium reacting with water?
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Metal + water → metal hydroxide + hydrogen; two water molecules balance the OH groups.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Iron is added to copper(II) sulfate solution. What is the solid that forms?
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Iron displaces copper, which forms as a pink-brown solid. The blue colour fades to pale green.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Why is there no reaction when iron is added to magnesium sulfate solution?
options: Iron is less reactive than magnesium
Iron is more reactive than magnesium
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: A less reactive metal cannot displace a more reactive one from its compound.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Magnesium is added to magnesium sulfate solution. Why is there no change?
options: Magnesium sulfate is not a salt
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Displacement needs a more reactive metal. A metal cannot be more reactive than itself.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Metal X displaces copper from copper(II) sulfate but does not displace aluminium from aluminium sulfate. What could X be?
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: X lies between aluminium and copper, so zinc or iron fit.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: In 3Mg + 2Al³⁺ → 3Mg²⁺ + 2Al, which statement is correct?
options: Magnesium is the reducing agent because it donates electrons
Magnesium is reduced because it gains electrons
Al³⁺ is the reducing agent because it gains electrons
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Magnesium loses electrons (is oxidised) and gives them to Al³⁺, so magnesium is the reducing agent.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Which is the balanced equation for the thermite reaction?
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: 2Al + Fe₂O₃ → Al₂O₃ + 2Fe: two Al, two Fe and three O on each side.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Why does aluminium displace iron from iron(III) oxide?
options: Iron is more reactive than aluminium
Aluminium is more reactive than iron
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: A more reactive metal takes the oxygen from the oxide of a less reactive metal.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: In the thermite reaction, which substance is reduced?
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Iron(III) oxide loses oxygen, so it is reduced. 'Iron is reduced' loses the mark — name the oxide.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: What does 'exothermic' mean?
options: Heat is given out to the surroundings
Heat is taken in from the surroundings
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Exothermic reactions give out heat (thermal energy). 'Energy released' on its own was ignored in 2024.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Why does aluminium resist corrosion even though it is quite high in the reactivity series?
options: It is coated in a thin protective layer of aluminium oxide
It is always alloyed with zinc
It does not react with oxygen
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: The tough oxide layer stops water and oxygen reaching the metal underneath.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Which property makes aluminium suitable for aircraft bodies?
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Aluminium has a low density (and its alloys are strong and resist corrosion), so aircraft are lighter.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Why is copper used for electrical wiring?
options: It has a low melting point
It is a very good electrical conductor and is ductile
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Copper conducts electricity very well and can be drawn into wires.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Why is copper used for water pipes?
options: It does not react with water
It is very hard and brittle
It dissolves slowly to clean the water
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Copper is unreactive — below hydrogen — so it does not react with water, and it is easy to bend.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Which type of steel is best for car body panels?
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Mild steel is soft and malleable, so it can be pressed into shape.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Which type of steel is best for a drill bit?
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: High-carbon steel is very hard, so it keeps a cutting edge, although it is brittle.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: What makes stainless steel suitable for cutlery?
options: It is soft and easily shaped
It contains a lot of carbon
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Stainless steel contains chromium (and nickel), so it does not rust.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Which is the best definition of an alloy?
options: A mixture of a metal and one or more other elements
A pure metal that has been heated
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: An alloy is a mixture, usually of a metal with other metals or carbon — not a compound.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Why is an alloy harder than the pure metal?
options: The alloy has stronger covalent bonds
Atoms of different sizes disrupt the layers, so they cannot slide easily
The alloy has no delocalised electrons
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Different-sized atoms distort the regular layers. Metals have no molecules and alloys still have delocalised electrons.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Why are pure metals malleable?
options: Their molecules are held by weak forces
Layers of atoms (ions) can slide over one another
They have a low melting point
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: Regular layers of identical positive ions slide over each other without the metallic bonding breaking.

13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.q: Which gives the correct order of reactivity, most reactive first?
13-reactivity-rusting-and-alloys.explain: From the series: magnesium, (aluminium, carbon), zinc, iron, (hydrogen), copper.

14-chemical-tests.q: Which is the correct test and result for hydrogen?
options: A lighted splint gives a squeaky pop
Damp red litmus paper turns blue
14-chemical-tests.explain: Hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop when a lighted splint is held near it. A glowing splint is the oxygen test.

14-chemical-tests.q: Which gas relights a glowing splint?
14-chemical-tests.explain: Oxygen helps things burn, so a glowing splint bursts back into flame.

14-chemical-tests.q: What is seen when carbon dioxide is bubbled through limewater?
14-chemical-tests.explain: Carbon dioxide reacts with calcium hydroxide to form insoluble calcium carbonate, which makes the limewater milky or cloudy.

14-chemical-tests.q: Which is the test for ammonia gas?
options: Damp blue litmus paper is bleached
Damp red litmus paper turns blue
14-chemical-tests.explain: Ammonia is an alkaline gas, so it turns damp red litmus paper blue.

14-chemical-tests.q: Which is the test for chlorine?
options: Damp blue litmus paper is bleached white
Damp red litmus paper turns blue
14-chemical-tests.explain: Chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper. Blue litmus may turn red first, but the bleaching is what identifies chlorine.

14-chemical-tests.q: Why must litmus paper be damp when testing a gas?
options: So that it does not catch fire
So that the gas can dissolve in the water and act as an acid or alkali
So that it sticks to the test tube
So that it changes colour more slowly
14-chemical-tests.explain: A gas has to dissolve in water before it can change the colour of an indicator.

14-chemical-tests.q: Which flame colour is produced by lithium ions?
14-chemical-tests.explain: Lithium ions give a red flame. Orange-red (brick-red) is calcium, and mark schemes reject it for lithium.

14-chemical-tests.q: Which flame colour is produced by sodium ions?
14-chemical-tests.explain: Sodium ions give a yellow flame.

14-chemical-tests.q: Which ion gives a lilac flame?
14-chemical-tests.explain: Potassium ions give a lilac (pale purple) flame.

14-chemical-tests.q: Which ion gives an orange-red flame?
14-chemical-tests.explain: Calcium ions give an orange-red flame, often called brick-red.

14-chemical-tests.q: Which flame colour is produced by copper(II) ions?
14-chemical-tests.explain: Copper(II) ions give a blue-green flame.

14-chemical-tests.q: How is a flame-test wire cleaned?
options: Wipe it with a paper towel
Rinse it in distilled water only
Dip it in sodium hydroxide solution
Dip it in concentrated hydrochloric acid and heat it until it gives no colour
14-chemical-tests.explain: Dipping in concentrated HCl and heating removes ions left from earlier tests, so they cannot mask the colour.

14-chemical-tests.q: Why is the flame-test wire cleaned before use?
options: To remove other ions that would mask or change the flame colour
14-chemical-tests.explain: Other ions on the wire would colour the flame too and interfere with the result.

14-chemical-tests.q: Which part of the Bunsen flame is used for a flame test?
options: The hottest part of the blue, non-luminous flame
Just above the top of the flame
The cool centre just above the barrel
14-chemical-tests.explain: The blue flame is hot and almost colourless, so it does not hide the colour from the ion.

14-chemical-tests.q: What is seen when sodium hydroxide solution is added to copper(II) sulfate solution?
14-chemical-tests.explain: Copper(II) hydroxide forms, which is an insoluble blue solid.

14-chemical-tests.q: What colour precipitate forms when sodium hydroxide solution is added to an iron(II) salt solution?
14-chemical-tests.explain: Iron(II) hydroxide, Fe(OH)₂, is a green precipitate.

14-chemical-tests.q: What colour precipitate forms when sodium hydroxide solution is added to an iron(III) salt solution?
14-chemical-tests.explain: Iron(III) hydroxide, Fe(OH)₃, is an orange-brown (red-brown) precipitate.

14-chemical-tests.q: Which is the correct ionic equation for the reaction of iron(III) ions with sodium hydroxide solution?
14-chemical-tests.explain: Three hydroxide ions balance the 3+ charge. Sodium ions are spectator ions and are left out.

14-chemical-tests.q: Which ionic equation shows the formation of the blue precipitate in the copper(II) ion test?
14-chemical-tests.explain: Copper(II) ions join two hydroxide ions to form insoluble copper(II) hydroxide.

14-chemical-tests.q: How is the test for ammonium ions carried out?
options: Add dilute acid and bubble the gas through limewater
Warm with sodium hydroxide solution and test the gas with damp red litmus paper
14-chemical-tests.explain: NaOH and warming release ammonia gas, which turns damp red litmus paper blue.

14-chemical-tests.q: In the ammonium test, why is the litmus paper held in the gas rather than dipped in the solution?
options: The solution contains sodium hydroxide, which is alkaline anyway
Litmus does not work in liquids
The solution would bleach the paper
14-chemical-tests.explain: Sodium hydroxide would turn red litmus blue on its own, so only testing the gas proves ammonia was made.

14-chemical-tests.q: Which ionic equation shows ammonium ions reacting with hydroxide ions?
14-chemical-tests.explain: The hydroxide ion takes an H⁺ from the ammonium ion, giving ammonia gas and water.

14-chemical-tests.q: Which reagents are used to test for chloride ions?
options: Dilute hydrochloric acid then barium chloride solution
Dilute sulfuric acid then silver nitrate solution
Dilute nitric acid then silver nitrate solution
Sodium hydroxide solution then silver nitrate solution
14-chemical-tests.explain: Halide ions are tested with nitric acid followed by silver nitrate solution.

14-chemical-tests.q: What colour precipitate do bromide ions give with acidified silver nitrate?
14-chemical-tests.explain: Silver bromide is a cream precipitate. Chloride gives white and iodide gives yellow.

14-chemical-tests.q: What colour precipitate do iodide ions give with acidified silver nitrate?
14-chemical-tests.explain: Silver iodide is a yellow precipitate.

14-chemical-tests.q: Why is hydrochloric acid NOT used to acidify the sample in the halide test?
options: It contains chloride ions that would form a white precipitate
14-chemical-tests.explain: Chloride from the acid would give white silver chloride whatever was in the sample.

14-chemical-tests.q: Why is the sample acidified before silver nitrate is added?
options: To make the precipitate a brighter colour
To remove carbonate ions that would also form a precipitate
14-chemical-tests.explain: Carbonate ions would give a precipitate with silver ions too; the acid removes them as carbon dioxide.

14-chemical-tests.q: Which ionic equation shows the formation of the precipitate in the chloride test?
14-chemical-tests.explain: Silver ions and chloride ions join to form insoluble white silver chloride.

14-chemical-tests.q: Which reagents are used to test for sulfate ions?
options: Dilute hydrochloric acid then barium chloride solution
Dilute nitric acid then silver nitrate solution
Dilute sulfuric acid then barium chloride solution
14-chemical-tests.explain: Sulfate ions give a white precipitate of barium sulfate with acidified barium chloride.

14-chemical-tests.q: Why is sulfuric acid NOT used to acidify the sample in the sulfate test?
options: It contains sulfate ions, so a white precipitate would always form
It reacts with barium to give a gas
It would turn the solution blue
14-chemical-tests.explain: Sulfate from the acid itself would form barium sulfate, giving a false positive.

14-chemical-tests.q: What is seen in a positive test for sulfate ions?
14-chemical-tests.explain: Barium sulfate is an insoluble white solid.

14-chemical-tests.q: Which ionic equation shows the formation of the precipitate in the sulfate test?
14-chemical-tests.explain: Barium ions and sulfate ions form insoluble barium sulfate.

14-chemical-tests.q: A solid fizzes when dilute hydrochloric acid is added, and the gas turns limewater milky. Which ion is present?
14-chemical-tests.explain: Carbonates react with acid to give carbon dioxide, which turns limewater milky.

14-chemical-tests.q: Which is the ionic equation for carbonate ions reacting with an acid?
14-chemical-tests.explain: Two hydrogen ions react with one carbonate ion to give carbon dioxide and water.

14-chemical-tests.q: Which chemical test shows that a liquid contains water?
options: It turns blue cobalt chloride blue
It turns anhydrous copper(II) sulfate from white to blue
14-chemical-tests.explain: Water turns white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate blue. The boiling point is a physical test, not a chemical one.

14-chemical-tests.q: Which is a physical test to show that a sample of water is pure?
options: Evaporate it and weigh the residue
Measure its boiling point — it should be exactly 100 °C
14-chemical-tests.explain: Pure water has a fixed boiling point of 100 °C (and freezing point of 0 °C).

14-chemical-tests.q: A sample of seawater is tested with anhydrous copper(II) sulfate. What is seen, and what does it show?
options: It turns blue; water is present, but not that the water is pure
It turns blue; the water is pure
It stays white; no water is present
It turns green; salt is present
14-chemical-tests.explain: The test only shows water is present. Dissolved salt does not stop the colour change, so it says nothing about purity.

14-chemical-tests.q: A solid gives a yellow flame, and its solution gives a white precipitate with dilute nitric acid and silver nitrate. What is the solid?
14-chemical-tests.explain: Yellow flame means sodium ions; white precipitate with acidified silver nitrate means chloride ions.

14-chemical-tests.q: A solution gives an orange-brown precipitate with sodium hydroxide, and a white precipitate with dilute hydrochloric acid and barium chloride. What is it?
14-chemical-tests.explain: Orange-brown hydroxide means iron(III) ions; white barium precipitate means sulfate ions.

14-chemical-tests.q: A white solid gives a red flame and fizzes with dilute acid, giving a gas that turns limewater milky. What is the solid?
14-chemical-tests.explain: A red flame means lithium; fizzing with a gas that turns limewater milky means carbonate. Calcium would give an orange-red flame.

15-energetics-and-equilibria.q: Which statement describes an exothermic reaction?
options: Heat energy is taken in from the surroundings
The products have more energy than the reactants
Heat energy is given out to the surroundings
The temperature of the surroundings falls
15-energetics-and-equilibria.explain: Exothermic means heat energy is given out to the surroundings, so the temperature rises. The products end up with less energy than the reactants.

15-energetics-and-equilibria.q: When ammonium nitrate dissolves in water, the temperature of the water falls. What type of change is this?
15-energetics-and-equilibria.explain: The temperature falls because heat energy is taken in from the water, so the change is endothermic.

15-energetics-and-equilibria.q: What is the sign of ΔH for an exothermic reaction?
15-energetics-and-equilibria.explain: In an exothermic reaction the chemicals lose energy to the surroundings, so ΔH is negative.

15-energetics-and-equilibria.q: In Q = mcΔT for a combustion experiment, what does m stand for?
options: The mass of the copper can
The relative formula mass of the fuel
15-energetics-and-equilibria.explain: Q is the heat taken in by the water, and c is the specific heat capacity of water, so m is the mass of water heated.

15-energetics-and-equilibria.q: 50 cm³ of solution rises in temperature by 10.0 °C. What is Q? (c = 4.2 J/g/°C)
15-energetics-and-equilibria.explain: Q = 50 × 4.2 × 10.0 = 2100 J, taking 1 cm³ of solution as 1 g.

15-energetics-and-equilibria.q: Q = 2.1 kJ is released when 0.010 mol of a reactant is used up and the temperature rises. What is ΔH?
15-energetics-and-equilibria.explain: ΔH = −Q ÷ n = −2.1 ÷ 0.010 = −210 kJ/mol. It is negative because the temperature rose.

15-energetics-and-equilibria.q: Why is a polystyrene cup used instead of a glass beaker in a neutralisation experiment?
options: Polystyrene is an insulator, so less heat is lost
Polystyrene conducts heat into the solution
15-energetics-and-equilibria.explain: Polystyrene is a poor conductor of heat, so less heat is lost to the surroundings. The mark scheme rejects 'no heat loss'.

15-energetics-and-equilibria.q: In a combustion experiment, why is the water in the copper can stirred?
options: To make the fuel burn faster
To spread the heat evenly through the water
15-energetics-and-equilibria.explain: Stirring distributes the heat evenly, so the thermometer reads the true temperature of all the water.

15-energetics-and-equilibria.q: A black solid forms on the bottom of the copper can above a burning fuel. What is it?
15-energetics-and-equilibria.explain: Soot is carbon, formed by incomplete combustion of the fuel when there is not enough oxygen.

15-energetics-and-equilibria.q: Which is NOT a reason why a measured enthalpy of combustion is smaller than the data-book value?
options: Heat is lost to the surroundings
15-energetics-and-equilibria.explain: Stirring improves accuracy. Heat loss, incomplete combustion and evaporation all make the measured value too small.

15-energetics-and-equilibria.q: Why should a spirit burner be reweighed immediately after the flame is put out?
options: The burner cools and gets lighter
The volatile fuel could evaporate, giving a false mass loss
The copper can would lose mass
15-energetics-and-equilibria.explain: Liquid fuels evaporate easily. Any fuel that evaporates would be counted as burned, making n too big.

15-energetics-and-equilibria.q: 0.12 g of magnesium (Ar 24) reacts completely. How many moles is this?
Excess zinc powder is added to copper(II) sulfate solution. Which moles should be used to calculate ΔH?
options: Moles of zinc plus copper(II) sulfate
15-energetics-and-equilibria.explain: The zinc is in excess, so the copper(II) sulfate is the reactant that is completely used up. Use its moles.

15-energetics-and-equilibria.q: In a neutralisation experiment the temperature rises from 21.0 °C to 34.7 °C. What is ΔT?
15-energetics-and-equilibria.explain: ΔT is the change: 34.7 − 21.0 = 13.7 °C. Using the final temperature is a common error.

15-energetics-and-equilibria.q: On an energy level diagram for an exothermic reaction, where are the products?
options: At the same level as the reactants
At the top of the hump
15-energetics-and-equilibria.explain: The chemicals lose energy in an exothermic reaction, so the products are at a lower energy than the reactants.

15-energetics-and-equilibria.q: On a reaction profile, the activation energy arrow goes from…
options: the products up to the peak
the reactants down to the products
the x-axis up to the peak
the reactants up to the peak
15-energetics-and-equilibria.explain: Activation energy is the energy needed to get from the reactants to the top of the hump, so the arrow starts at the reactants level and points up.

15-energetics-and-equilibria.q: How does a catalysed reaction profile compare with the uncatalysed one?
options: Lower peak, same reactant and product levels
Higher peak, same reactant and product levels
15-energetics-and-equilibria.explain: A catalyst provides a pathway with a lower activation energy, so the peak is lower. The reactants and products, and so ΔH, are unchanged.

15-energetics-and-equilibria.q: What effect does a catalyst have on ΔH for a reaction?
15-energetics-and-equilibria.explain: The reactants and products have the same energies with or without a catalyst, so ΔH does not change.

15-energetics-and-equilibria.q: Which statement about bonds is correct?
options: Bond breaking and making both take in energy
Bond breaking takes in energy and bond making gives out energy
15-energetics-and-equilibria.explain: Energy is needed to pull atoms apart (endothermic). Energy is released when new bonds form (exothermic).

15-energetics-and-equilibria.q: How is ΔH calculated from bond energies?
15-energetics-and-equilibria.explain: ΔH = energy taken in breaking bonds minus energy given out making bonds. A negative answer means exothermic.

15-energetics-and-equilibria.q: H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl. H–H 436, Cl–Cl 242, H–Cl 431 kJ/mol. What is ΔH?
A reaction is exothermic. What must be true about its bonds?
options: More energy is released making bonds than is taken in breaking bonds
More energy is taken in breaking bonds than is released making bonds
The same bonds are broken and made
15-energetics-and-equilibria.explain: If bond making releases more energy than bond breaking takes in, there is a net release of energy, so ΔH is negative.

15-energetics-and-equilibria.q: Why is ΔH for making an ester from ethanoic acid and ethanol approximately 0 kJ/mol?
options: The same bonds are broken and made
15-energetics-and-equilibria.explain: One C–O and one O–H bond are broken and one C–O and one O–H bond are made, so the energy in equals the energy out.

15-energetics-and-equilibria.q: How many O–H bonds are made in 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O?
15-energetics-and-equilibria.explain: Each water molecule has two O–H bonds, and there are two water molecules, so four O–H bonds are made.

15-energetics-and-equilibria.q: What does the symbol ⇌ show in an equation?
15-energetics-and-equilibria.explain: ⇌ means the reaction can go in both directions: the products can react to re-form the reactants.

15-energetics-and-equilibria.q: What colour change happens when hydrated copper(II) sulfate is heated?
15-energetics-and-equilibria.explain: Heating removes the water of crystallisation. Blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate becomes white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate.

15-energetics-and-equilibria.q: Which substance is used to test whether a liquid contains water?
options: Hydrated copper(II) sulfate, which turns white
Anhydrous copper(II) sulfate, which turns blue
15-energetics-and-equilibria.explain: Water turns white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate blue. Hydrated copper(II) sulfate is already blue.

15-energetics-and-equilibria.q: Ammonium chloride is heated at the bottom of a test tube. What is seen near the cooler top of the tube?
15-energetics-and-equilibria.explain: NH₄Cl ⇌ NH₃ + HCl. The gases recombine in the cooler part of the tube to form white ammonium chloride again.

15-energetics-and-equilibria.q: Which equation shows the effect of heat on ammonium chloride?
15-energetics-and-equilibria.explain: Ammonium chloride decomposes into ammonia and hydrogen chloride, and the reaction is reversible.

15-energetics-and-equilibria.q: Which is a characteristic of a reaction at dynamic equilibrium?
options: The concentrations of reactants and products are equal
The forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate
15-energetics-and-equilibria.explain: At dynamic equilibrium both reactions continue at the same rate. 'Concentrations are equal' is rejected by mark schemes.

15-energetics-and-equilibria.q: At dynamic equilibrium, the concentrations of reactants and products…
15-energetics-and-equilibria.explain: Because the forward and reverse rates are equal, the concentrations stop changing. They are constant, not necessarily equal.

15-energetics-and-equilibria.q: Why must a reversible reaction be in a sealed container to reach dynamic equilibrium?
options: So that no reactants or products escape
So that air can get in
15-energetics-and-equilibria.explain: If a product escapes, the reverse reaction cannot happen, so equilibrium is never reached.

15-energetics-and-equilibria.q: What is the effect of a catalyst on the position of equilibrium?
options: No effect, but equilibrium is reached sooner
It shifts towards the exothermic side
15-energetics-and-equilibria.explain: A catalyst increases the rates of the forward and backward reactions equally, so the position does not change.

15-energetics-and-equilibria.q: Why does a catalyst not change the yield of a reversible reaction?
options: It is used up in the reaction
It only speeds up the forward reaction
It increases the rates of the forward and backward reactions equally
15-energetics-and-equilibria.explain: Both rates rise by the same amount, so they stay equal at the same concentrations. The yield is unchanged.

15-energetics-and-equilibria.q: Increasing the temperature shifts the position of equilibrium in which direction?
15-energetics-and-equilibria.explain: A rise in temperature shifts equilibrium in the direction of the endothermic reaction.

15-energetics-and-equilibria.q: CH₄(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO(g) + 3H₂(g), ΔH = +206 kJ/mol. What happens to the yield of hydrogen if the temperature is lowered?
15-energetics-and-equilibria.explain: The forward reaction is endothermic. Lowering the temperature shifts equilibrium in the exothermic direction, to the left, so less hydrogen.

15-energetics-and-equilibria.q: For CH₄(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO(g) + 3H₂(g), what happens to the yield of hydrogen if the pressure is lowered?
15-energetics-and-equilibria.explain: There are 2 moles of gas on the left and 4 on the right. Lower pressure shifts equilibrium to more moles of gas, the right, so more hydrogen.

15-energetics-and-equilibria.q: 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g). Increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium…
options: to the right, because there are fewer moles of gas on the right
to the left, because there are fewer moles of gas on the left
to the right, because the reaction is exothermic
nowhere, because pressure has no effect
15-energetics-and-equilibria.explain: There are 3 moles of gas on the left and 2 on the right. Higher pressure shifts equilibrium towards fewer moles of gas.

15-energetics-and-equilibria.q: H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g). What is the effect of increasing the pressure on the position of equilibrium?
15-energetics-and-equilibria.explain: There are 2 moles of gas on each side, so changing the pressure does not favour either side.

15-energetics-and-equilibria.q: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ has a negative ΔH. What happens to the yield of ammonia if the temperature is increased?
options: It increases then stays the same
15-energetics-and-equilibria.explain: The forward reaction is exothermic, so the reverse is endothermic. Heating shifts equilibrium to the left, so less ammonia.

16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.q: What is the functional group of the alkenes?
16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.explain: Alkenes all contain the carbon–carbon double bond, >C=C<. –OH is the alcohol group and –COOH the carboxylic acid group.

16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.q: What is the general formula of the alkenes?
16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.explain: Alkenes have twice as many H atoms as C atoms, CₙH₂ₙ. CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ is the alkanes.

16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.q: What is the molecular formula of propene?
16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.explain: Propene has 3 carbons and fits CₙH₂ₙ, so it is C₃H₆. C₃H₈ is propane.

16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.q: Why is ethene described as unsaturated?
options: It contains only carbon and hydrogen
It is a gas at room temperature
It contains a carbon–carbon double bond
16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.explain: Unsaturated means it contains a C=C double bond. 'Only carbon and hydrogen' is what makes it a hydrocarbon.

16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.q: Which statement is the definition of a hydrocarbon?
options: A compound containing hydrogen and carbon atoms only
A compound containing hydrogen and carbon molecules
An element made of carbon and hydrogen
A compound containing carbon, hydrogen and oxygen
16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.explain: A hydrocarbon is a compound of hydrogen and carbon atoms only. Mark schemes reject 'molecules' and 'element' here.

16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.q: What is the empirical formula of every alkene?
16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.explain: CₙH₂ₙ always simplifies to a 1 : 2 ratio of C to H, so the empirical formula is CH₂.

16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.q: Bromine water is added to an alkene and shaken. What colour change is seen?
16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.explain: The bromine adds across the C=C and is used up, so the orange bromine water is decolourised.

16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.q: Bromine water is shaken with an alkane at room temperature, in the dark. What is observed?
16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.explain: Alkanes are saturated, so there is no C=C to add to. They only react with bromine in UV light, by substitution.

16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.q: What is the product when ethene reacts with bromine?
16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.explain: C₂H₄ + Br₂ → C₂H₄Br₂. One Br adds to each carbon of the double bond, giving 1,2-dibromoethane as the only product.

16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.q: What type of reaction happens between ethene and bromine?
16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.explain: Two molecules join into one and the C=C opens, so it is addition. Substitution is the alkane reaction.

16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.q: Which condition is needed for ethane to react with bromine?
16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.explain: Alkanes react with halogens only in UV light, by substitution. Alkenes need no UV.

16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.q: Which are the products of the reaction between ethane and bromine in UV light?
16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.explain: C₂H₆ + Br₂ → C₂H₅Br + HBr. One H is swapped for a Br, and the H leaves as hydrogen bromide.

16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.q: But-1-ene reacts with bromine. What is the molecular formula of the product?
16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.explain: Addition keeps every atom: C₄H₈ + Br₂ → C₄H₈Br₂. No hydrogen is lost.

16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.q: What is the structural formula of but-2-ene?
16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.explain: In but-2-ene the double bond is between carbons 2 and 3, in the middle of the chain. CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃ is but-1-ene.

16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.q: What is the structural formula of but-1-ene?
16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.explain: But-1-ene has four carbons with the double bond starting at carbon 1. CH₂=CHCH₃ is propene.

16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.q: What is meant by the term isomers?
options: Compounds with the same empirical formula and the same structure
Compounds with the same chemical formula
Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons
Compounds with the same molecular formula but different structural formulae
16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.explain: Isomers share a molecular formula but have different arrangements of atoms. 'Chemical formula' was rejected by the mark scheme.

16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.q: Which pair of compounds are isomers?
16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.explain: Both are C₄H₈ with the C=C in different positions. The other pairs have different molecular formulae.

16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.q: Which compound is saturated but still fits the formula CₙH₂ₙ?
options: A ring of four carbon atoms joined by single bonds
16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.explain: A four-carbon ring is C₄H₈ but has only single bonds, so it is saturated. Real papers have used this as a trick.

16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.q: How many pairs of electrons are shared between the two carbon atoms in ethene?
16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.explain: A double bond is two shared pairs, four electrons in total. Each C–H bond is one shared pair.

16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.q: Which is the correct way to describe a test to show a compound is unsaturated?
options: Add bromine and it goes clear
Add bromine water and it changes colour
Add bromine water in UV light and it turns colourless
Add bromine water and it turns from orange to colourless
16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.explain: The reagent must be bromine water and the result must be colourless. 'Clear' and 'changes colour' score nothing, and UV is wrong for alkenes.

16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.q: What is a monomer?
options: A small molecule that joins with many others to form a polymer
The part of a polymer shown in brackets
16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.explain: Monomers are the small molecules, such as ethene, that join together to make a polymer.

16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.q: Which of these substances can be used to form an addition polymer?
16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.explain: An addition polymer needs a monomer with a C=C. Ethene has one; methane and ethane are saturated.

16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.q: What happens to the C=C double bond of each monomer during addition polymerisation?
options: It stays in the polymer chain
It opens up so the monomers can join together
It is broken and water is released
16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.explain: Each double bond opens to a single bond, freeing a bond on each carbon to link to the next monomer. No water is made in addition polymerisation.

16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.q: What is the name of the polymer made from CH₂=CHCl?
16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.explain: CH₂=CHCl is chloroethene, so its polymer is poly(chloroethene).

16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.q: Which monomer is used to make PTFE?
16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.explain: PTFE is poly(tetrafluoroethene). Its monomer tetrafluoroethene has four F atoms: CF₂=CF₂.

16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.q: Which is the repeat unit of poly(propene)?
16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.explain: Only the two C=C carbons form the chain. The third carbon stays as a CH₃ branch.

16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.q: A student draws a repeat unit without the bonds sticking out through the brackets. What is wrong?
options: The n should be inside the brackets
16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.explain: A repeat unit needs an extension bond out of each side. The 2023 scheme rejected a structure without them.

16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.q: How many carbon atoms are in the main chain of one poly(propene) repeat unit?
16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.explain: The two carbons from the C=C form the main chain. The CH₃ carbon is a side branch.

16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.q: A repeat unit contains two carbons, each bonded to two F atoms. What is the monomer?
16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.explain: Put a C=C between the two chain carbons and keep the four F atoms: CF₂=CF₂, tetrafluoroethene. The -ane name has no double bond.

16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.q: A repeat unit is –CH₂–CHCl–. Which monomer was used?
16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.explain: Put a double bond between the two chain carbons: CH₂=CHCl, chloroethene. Chloroethane has no C=C, and chloropropene has three carbons.

16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.q: What is the Mᵣ of chloroethene, C₂H₃Cl? [C = 12, H = 1, Cl = 35.5]
A poly(ethene) molecule has Mᵣ = 56 000. About how many ethene monomers made it? [C = 12, H = 1]
What is the empirical formula of poly(ethene)?
16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.explain: An addition polymer has the same atom ratio as its monomer. Ethene C₂H₄ simplifies to CH₂.

16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.q: Why does poly(ethene) not decolourise bromine water?
options: It is saturated — its C=C bonds were used up in polymerisation
16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.explain: The double bonds opened to make the chain, so the polymer has only single bonds and cannot add bromine.

16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.q: Why do addition polymers cause problems in landfill sites?
options: They react with rainwater to form acids
They release oxygen as they rot
They are inert and do not biodegrade
16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.explain: Addition polymers are inert and non-biodegradable, so they stay in landfill for hundreds of years and the sites fill up.

16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.q: Which is an environmental problem of burning addition polymers?
16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.explain: Burning releases toxic gases such as carbon monoxide (and hydrogen chloride from poly(chloroethene)), plus CO₂. The ozone layer is the wrong idea and was penalised.

16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.q: Which toxic gas can be produced by burning poly(chloroethene) but not poly(ethene)?
16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.explain: Only poly(chloroethene) contains chlorine, which ends up as hydrogen chloride. Either polymer can give CO and CO₂.

16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.q: Which reaction is a substitution reaction?
16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.explain: In CH₄ + Cl₂, one H is replaced by Cl and HCl is made — substitution. The others are addition, combustion and addition polymerisation.

16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.q: Which type of reaction is 2C₃H₆ + 9O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O?
16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.explain: Burning in oxygen to give carbon dioxide and water is combustion.

16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.q: Why is there only one product when an addition polymer forms?
options: A catalyst removes the other products
Every atom of every monomer ends up in the polymer
16-alkenes-and-addition-polymers.explain: In addition polymerisation the monomers join whole and nothing is removed. Condensation polymers (module 17) also make water.

17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.q: Which functional group is found in all alcohols?
17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.explain: Alcohols contain the –OH group. –COOH is a carboxylic acid, –COO– is an ester and C=C is an alkene.

17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.q: Which is the functional group of a carboxylic acid?
17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.explain: Carboxylic acids contain –COOH: a carbon with a double-bonded O and an O–H.

17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.q: Which functional group is found in an ester?
17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.explain: Esters contain the –COO– group, where the single-bonded O joins to another carbon instead of H.

17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.q: What is the molecular formula of ethanol?
17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.explain: A molecular formula just counts atoms: 2 C, 6 H, 1 O. A 2022 mark scheme rejected C₂H₅OH for this.

17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.q: What is the structural formula of propan-1-ol?
17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.explain: Propan-1-ol has three carbons with the –OH on the end carbon.

17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.q: What is the molecular formula of butan-1-ol?
17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.explain: CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH has 4 C, 10 H and 1 O.

17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.q: Which statement about a homologous series is correct?
options: Members have the same chemical properties and the same boiling point
Members have the same molecular formula
Members have the same general formula and similar chemical properties
17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.explain: Same general formula and similar chemical properties. Consecutive members differ by CH₂, and boiling points show a trend.

17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.q: Ethanol is heated with acidified potassium dichromate(VI). What is the colour change?
17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.explain: The dichromate(VI) changes from orange to green as it oxidises the ethanol. The order matters.

17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.q: Methanol is heated with potassium dichromate(VI) and one other reagent. What is the other reagent?
17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.explain: The dichromate is used in dilute sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄), as in 2024 Edexcel 2C Q5(b)(i).

17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.q: Which product forms when ethanol is oxidised by potassium dichromate(VI)?
17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.explain: Ethanol is oxidised to ethanoic acid. The carbon count stays at two.

17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.q: Wine left open to the air turns sour. Why?
options: Microbes use oxygen to oxidise ethanol to ethanoic acid
17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.explain: This is microbial oxidation. Oxygen in the air is used to turn ethanol into ethanoic acid, which gives vinegar.

17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.q: What is vinegar?
options: An aqueous solution containing ethanoic acid
17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.explain: Vinegar is an aqueous solution containing ethanoic acid.

17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.q: Which is the balanced equation for the complete combustion of ethanol?
17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.explain: The alcohol already has one O. Seven O are needed on the right (4 + 3), so 6 come from 3O₂.

17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.q: What are the conditions for making ethanol by hydration of ethene?
17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.explain: Ethene and steam react at about 300 °C and 60–70 atm over a phosphoric acid catalyst.

17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.q: What is the catalyst in fermentation?
17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.explain: Fermentation uses enzymes in yeast at about 30 °C.

17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.q: Which is the balanced equation for fermentation?
17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.explain: One glucose gives two ethanol and two carbon dioxide: 6 C, 12 H and 6 O on each side.

17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.q: Why is fermentation carried out in the absence of air?
options: Nitrogen would react with the glucose
Air would make the enzymes work too fast
Oxygen would oxidise the ethanol to ethanoic acid
17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.explain: With oxygen present, ethanol is oxidised to ethanoic acid. Aerobic respiration would also give only CO₂ and water.

17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.q: Why is fermentation not carried out at 60 °C?
options: The enzymes in the yeast would denature
17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.explain: Above the optimum of about 30 °C the enzymes' active sites change shape, so they stop working.

17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.q: Which is an advantage of fermentation compared with hydration of ethene?
options: It uses a renewable raw material
17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.explain: Glucose comes from plants, which are renewable. Ethene comes from finite crude oil. The other three are advantages of hydration.

17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.q: Which is a disadvantage of fermentation compared with hydration?
options: It is a slow batch process
17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.explain: Fermentation is slow and runs in batches, and the ethanol has to be purified.

17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.q: What is the name of CH₃CH₂COOH?
17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.explain: Count all three carbons, including the one in –COOH: propanoic acid.

17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.q: What is the structural formula of methanoic acid?
17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.explain: Methanoic acid has one carbon, which carries an H, a C=O and an O–H.

17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.q: What is the molecular formula of butanoic acid?
17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.explain: CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH has 4 C, 8 H and 2 O.

17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.q: What are the products when ethanoic acid reacts with magnesium?
options: Magnesium ethanoate, water and carbon dioxide
17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.explain: Acid + metal → salt + hydrogen. The salt of ethanoic acid is an ethanoate.

17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.q: What are the products when methanoic acid reacts with sodium carbonate?
options: Sodium methanoate, water and carbon dioxide
17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.explain: Acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide: 2HCOOH + Na₂CO₃ → 2HCOONa + H₂O + CO₂.

17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.q: What is the formula of sodium ethanoate?
17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.explain: Sodium replaces the H of the –COOH. A mark scheme rejected NaCOOH for sodium methanoate.

17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.q: Which test shows that a liquid contains ethanoic acid rather than ethanol?
17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.explain: Carboxylic acids fizz with carbonates (and metals such as magnesium). Alcohols do not.

17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.q: What is needed to make ethyl ethanoate from ethanol and ethanoic acid?
options: A few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid, warmed
17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.explain: Concentrated sulfuric acid is the catalyst. The mixture is warmed in a water bath.

17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.q: Why does the amount of concentrated sulfuric acid stay the same when an ester is made?
options: It is too concentrated to react
It is a product as well as a reactant
17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.explain: A catalyst speeds up the reaction without being used up, so its moles do not change.

17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.q: What is the name of the ester CH₃COOCH₂CH₃?
17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.explain: The C=O side has 2 carbons (ethanoate) and the O side has 2 carbons (ethyl).

17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.q: What is the name of the ester made from propanol and methanoic acid?
17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.explain: Alcohol part first with -yl (propyl), then acid part with -oate (methanoate).

17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.q: What is the name of the ester CH₃COOCH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃?
17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.explain: CH₃CO– is the ethanoate part and –CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃ is butyl: butyl ethanoate (2024 Edexcel 2C Q5(d)).

17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.q: What is the molecular formula of butyl ethanoate?
17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.explain: CH₃COOCH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃ has 6 C, 12 H and 2 O.

17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.q: Which alcohol and acid react to make methyl propanoate?
17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.explain: 'Methyl' comes from the alcohol (methanol) and 'propanoate' from the acid (propanoic acid).

17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.q: Why are esters used in perfumes and food flavourings?
options: They are unreactive and have no smell
They are volatile and have distinctive smells
They dissolve in water to form alkalis
17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.explain: Esters evaporate easily and have distinctive, often fruity, smells.

17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.q: In the ester practical, the mixture is poured into sodium carbonate solution. How do you know an ester has formed?
options: A fruity smell and an oily layer on the surface
17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.explain: The ester is a fruity-smelling oily layer. The fizzing is only the carbonate reacting with leftover acid.

17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.q: Which pair of monomers can form a polyester?
options: A dicarboxylic acid and a diol
17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.explain: Each monomer needs a functional group at both ends, so the chain keeps growing. Ethanol + ethanoic acid only make one ester molecule.

17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.q: What else is made when ethanedioic acid and ethanediol form a polyester?
17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.explain: Condensation polymerisation gives out one water molecule for each ester link formed.

17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.q: When a dicarboxylic acid and a diol join, which atoms are lost as water?
options: –OH from the acid and –H from the diol
–H from the acid and –OH from the diol
17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.explain: The acid loses –OH from its –COOH and the diol loses H from its –OH. They combine as H₂O.

17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.q: What is special about biopolyesters?
options: They are made by addition polymerisation
They are made from crude oil
They cannot be broken down by microorganisms
17-alcohols-acids-esters-and-polyesters.explain: Biopolyesters are biodegradable. Microorganisms break them down, so they cause fewer disposal problems.
